statement: In one controlled study (McCann et al., 1994), lumbar cerebrospinal fluid 5-HIAA, the main breakdown product of serotonin, was lower in 30 people who had used MDMA at least 25 times than in 28 controls: 10.3 (SD 3.1) against 15.2 (7.9) ng/ml, about a third lower (editors' calculation), F(1, 54) = 11.6, p = .001 after adjustment for age and height. The difference depended on sex: 46% lower in women (12 against 11 people), marked significant, and 20% lower in men (18 against 17), not marked significant. 5-HIAA was not related to the number of MDMA exposures (r = -0.2, p = .33), the duration or frequency of use, or the time since last use. The MDMA group had used other drugs far more often (for example cocaine 80% against 29%, LSD and other hallucinogens 87% against 32%), which was not adjusted for, although the Discussion describes the groups as matched for other drug use; no one was measured before use; and the authors write that the nature of the alteration is difficult to establish from cerebrospinal fluid data alone. Prolactin responses to L-tryptophan and pain sensitivity showed no group differences, and the MDMA group scored as less impulsive and less hostile on two personality scales.
plain: One 1994 study measured a breakdown product of serotonin in spinal fluid. It was about a third lower in 30 people who had used MDMA many times than in 28 people who had not, clearly in the women but not in the men. The MDMA group had also used many other drugs far more often, which was not taken into account, and nobody was measured before they started. A lower level cannot show whether serotonin nerve cells were damaged.

statement: In cross-sectional studies, people who use ecstasy score lower on average than people who do not on some memory and executive tests, but the size of the difference is uncertain and the pattern differs across tasks and studies. A 2026 meta-analysis rated critically low confidence pooled four or five small studies per comparison: overall learning and memory was lower in people abstinent for at least 6 months (g -1.37, 95% CI -2.65 to -0.09; I2 96%) and in people currently using (g -1.06, -1.98 to -0.15; I2 95%) than in MDMA-naive comparison groups, while the intervals for the verbal-memory subtests all included zero (Ung et al., 2026). A 2009 review of 33 studies rated critically low confidence, which pooled no effect sizes, found deficits mainly in updating information in working memory and in visuospatial tasks with high executive demand, little evidence of impaired shifting or inhibition, and contradictory results on access to long-term memory; most of the updating studies came from the review's own authors, with overlapping samples (Murphy et al., 2009). Narrative reviews describe the memory deficits as larger and more consistent (Parrott, 2011, 2013). In almost every study both groups had used other drugs, most often cannabis, and people were tested once, after use had begun, so differences that predate use cannot be excluded.
plain: On average, people who use ecstasy score lower on some memory and thinking tests than people who don't. How much lower is very uncertain, and results differ a lot between studies and tasks. Almost all studies tested people once, after they had started, and most also used other drugs such as cannabis, so the tests cannot show that ecstasy caused the difference.

statement: In the one study read that selected people who had used ecstasy but little else (Halpern et al., 2011), 52 people from the Salt Lake City all-night dance scene who had used ecstasy (a median of 43.5 lifetime episodes; last use a median of 121 days earlier), screened for other drugs by interview and by breath, urine and hair tests, were compared with 59 people from the same scene who had not used it. Memory measures did not differ after adjustment (verbal learning, difference -0.5, 95% CI -4.2 to 3.2). Of 15 tests, four differed between the whole groups at p < .05 without correction for multiple comparisons (vocabulary, digit symbol, spatial span forward, non-dominant-hand pegboard) and two were borderline (p = .05); in the 22 people with more than 50 episodes, scores were lower on a strategy-application test (79.5% against 88.5% of brief items, p = .003, virtually unchanged after adjustment for verbal IQ and depression), and more lifetime episodes went with fewer brief items within the ecstasy group (r = -0.37). The authors read the lower vocabulary as a difference that predates use, and the strategy finding as possibly reflecting impulsivity that may also predate use. For the heavier-use subgroup, a large effect (d 0.8) was excluded on all 14 chosen measures but a medium one (d 0.5) on only 6 of them, although the authors say many, and only 6 people had used 150 times or more. The groups also differed in parents' education, ethnicity, number of all-night parties and cannabis use. Two commentaries read the same results in opposite ways (Parrott, 2011; Lyvers, 2011).
plain: One US study picked people who had used ecstasy but hardly any other drugs, checked with breath, urine and hair tests, and compared them with people from the same dance scene who had never used it. Memory did not differ, and most of the 15 tests were similar. People who had used it more than 50 times did worse on one planning test. Nobody was tested before they started, and medium-sized differences could not be ruled out on most tests.

statement: In the one prospective cohort read (Schilt et al., 2007, in the Netherlands), 58 young adults who started using ecstasy after a first test and 60 who did not showed no differences on any of 12 test scores before any use. At retest, after very little use (a median of 1.5 tablets in total; last use a median of about 8 weeks before), verbal learning improved less in those who started (immediate recall +0.86 against +3.90 words; adjusted difference 2.23, 95% CI 0.17 to 4.29, p = .03), delayed recall changed by -0.52 against +0.65 words (0.63, 0.05 to 1.22, p = .03), and more showed any decline in recognition (22% against 7%; odds ratio 5.87, p = .02); nine other scores did not differ. All scores stayed within the normal range. The delayed-recall difference remained after excluding everyone who had used cocaine or amphetamines (43 against 57 people). The groups differed in cannabis use (higher before and after in those who started) and in cocaine use at follow-up, and in time between tests (11.1 against 19.1 months), and in the wider cohort people who started scored higher on sensation seeking. A second prospective cohort is described here only by a narrative review (Parrott, 2013), which also misstates this cohort's retest interval.
plain: A Dutch study tested young people before they had ever used ecstasy, and again 1 to 2 years later. Those who had started, mostly with very little use, improved less on a word-memory test than those who had not. All scores stayed in the normal range. The groups also differed in cannabis and cocaine use and in how long they waited between tests, so this does not show that ecstasy caused it.

debate.question: Does recreational MDMA use damage dopamine nerve cells in people?
debate.evidence_yes: The case for a dopamine effect rested on the 2002 primate report of severe dopaminergic neurotoxicity after what its title called a common recreational dose regimen, and on its authors' argument that the pattern of dosing, not only the amount, decides which transmitter systems are affected, so that three doses given over several hours produced damage to both dopamine and serotonin systems while more widely spaced, higher doses produced serotonin damage alone (Ricaurte and colleagues, reply to Mithoefer et al., 2003). They also pointed to mouse evidence of MDMA-related dopamine neurotoxicity, and argued that human studies which ignore patterns of use would not be expected to show differences in dopamine markers. That report was retracted in September 2003 (as described by Barnett and Doblin, 2021), so this side of the argument no longer has its primary support.
debate.evidence_no: The critics cited human studies finding normal dopamine with reduced serotonin in people who used MDMA heavily: two in vivo imaging studies of the dopamine transporter, one post-mortem examination, and earlier work by the same research group reporting dopamine metabolites in cerebrospinal fluid that were not reduced (Mithoefer et al., 2003). They also argued that the high mortality among the primates showed the regimen was not a common recreational one. The newspaper case study states that evidence of MDMA-induced dopaminergic toxicity in humans has not appeared in the years since the retraction (Barnett and Doblin, 2021).
debate.neither_can_show: Of the human studies on either side, only one cerebrospinal fluid study was read for this claim (McCann et al., 1994), and neither the 2002 paper nor its retraction notice is among the sources. Both documents are partisan: one letter is from people who ran and defended the study, the other from an organization that funds MDMA therapy research and asked for an investigation. The critics' description of the cerebrospinal fluid literature is not accurate for at least one study they cite, in which the dopamine metabolite homovanillic acid was lower in the MDMA group overall and in women (see card sc_mithoefer_2003). A statement that evidence has not materialized is an argument from silence: no systematic search is reported behind it.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). The claim that recreational MDMA damages dopamine neurons in people rested on a study that was withdrawn because the animals had mostly received a different drug, and no human evidence for it has been put before us. That is not the same as showing that MDMA leaves dopamine systems untouched: the human studies cited on both sides have not been read here, their samples were small and unselected for pattern of use, and the markers used (transporter binding, a metabolite in spinal fluid) can change without loss of nerve cells. The honest position is that the question is open and that the burden rests with anyone asserting either answer.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Dopamine transporter or vesicular transporter imaging, and post-mortem dopamine markers, in people with documented heavy MDMA use and little stimulant use, against matched controls, with the pattern of use recorded and repeat measurement over abstinence; and a systematic search of the human literature published since 2003, which none of the sources read here reports.

statement: Whether recreational ecstasy use causes lasting damage to the serotonin system in people, and whether any such damage explains the lower test scores found in people who use it, is contested and not settled by the sources read here. On one side, reviews report lower serotonin transporter binding in most imaging studies (second-hand here) and lower memory and executive scores in many studies, often related to lifetime use; one controlled study found cerebrospinal fluid 5-HIAA about a third lower, clearly in women only (McCann et al., 1994); and the one prospective cohort read found a smaller gain in verbal learning after very little use (Schilt et al., 2007). On the other, the 5-HIAA difference was unrelated to amount or recency of use and confounded by much heavier use of other drugs; the prospective cohort's scores stayed in the normal range and its groups differed in cannabis and cocaine use; the study that selected people who used little else found memory unchanged and most tests similar (Halpern et al., 2011); traits such as impulsivity predict who starts; and the reviews' descriptions of individual studies are at points inaccurate. The two reviews with systematic searches were rated critically low confidence (Murphy et al., 2009; Ung et al., 2026), and authors on both sides call for prospective studies with brain measures. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Does ecstasy damage the brain's serotonin system for good? Experts disagree, and the papers read here are opinion pieces and reviews, not new studies. Nobody has tested people before they started using, so a difference found later could have been there all along.
comparator: People who have not used ecstasy
outcome: Lasting damage to serotonin neurons, and cognitive consequences attributed to it
magnitude: Not estimable. Transporter binding figures are second-hand (lower by 19% to 46% across cortical regions in one study, as summarized by Parrott, 2013).

risk_of_bias.note: The narrative reviews, letters and commentaries appraise nothing and select partisanly; the primary studies are cross-sectional or, in one case, a small cohort, with confounding by other drug use (cards sc_mccann_1994, sc_halpern_2011, sc_schilt_2007); both systematic reviews are rated critically low confidence.

debate.question: Does recreational ecstasy use cause lasting damage to the brain's serotonin system in people, and does that damage explain the lower test scores found in people who use it?
debate.evidence_yes: A narrative review sets out the case: serotonergic neurotoxicity after MDMA is well established in laboratory animals; most human imaging studies report lower serotonin transporter binding in people abstinent from ecstasy, by 19% to 46% across cortical regions and 21% in the hippocampus in one study of 49 people against 50 (as summarized), related to lifetime use and surviving control for other drug use; a group preferring MDMA showed reductions while a group preferring hallucinogens showed none; memory and higher cognitive differences appear in many studies, with meta-analytic differences of about 0.3 to 1.0 SD, and are reported in relation to lifetime dose; and lower binding goes with poorer memory in two imaging studies (Parrott, 2013). A letter adds that differences appear even in people who use almost no other drugs, and reads this as showing damage under conditions the author calls protective (Parrott, 2011). The author of a cross-sectional imaging study holds that MDMA's serotonin neurotoxicity in non-human primates is well established, that he knows of no evidence that humans are less vulnerable, and that incident use was followed by increased impulsivity in a prospective cohort (Cowan, 2012). Primary studies read here add: cerebrospinal fluid 5-HIAA about a third lower in people who had used MDMA many times, clearly in women (McCann et al., 1994); a smaller gain in verbal learning in people who started using, against people who did not, in a cohort tested before first use (Schilt et al., 2007); and lower learning and memory scores in people abstinent for at least 6 months, as in people currently using, against MDMA-naive groups (Ung et al., 2026).
debate.evidence_no: Only one cohort read here tested people before they began using, and only after very little use (Schilt et al., 2007); the other studies cannot exclude differences that predate use; traits such as impulsivity and weaker executive control are linked to lower serotonergic function and to heavier substance use, and decision-making predicted first ecstasy use in a prospective study, so the heaviest-using groups would score lower even with no drug effect (Lyvers, 2011). In the study designed to remove confounding by other drugs, only one of 15 tests clearly differed, and only in the heavier-use subgroup (Lyvers, 2011). Transporter binding in people who use ecstasy appears to recover with abstinence, unlike the persistent reductions reported years after fenfluramine, a drug prescribed to millions (Lyvers, 2011). Re-analysis of one imaging study's raw data, combining the MDMA group with controls, found no association between exposure and brain activation (as reported by Cowan, 2012). Not every imaging study finds reductions, and a prospective cohort of people with very low use found no transporter difference (Parrott, 2013). The animal literature itself admits an interpretation without loss of nerve terminals, and the field has been criticized for lacking a clear definition of neurotoxicity (Parrott, 2013). In the primary studies read here: the study that selected people who used little else found memory unchanged and most tests similar, with a large effect excluded on every measure (Halpern et al., 2011); the 5-HIAA difference was unrelated to number of exposures, duration, frequency or recency of use, and the MDMA group had used cocaine and hallucinogens far more often (McCann et al., 1994); and the prospective cohort's scores stayed in the normal range, with groups that differed in cannabis and cocaine use and in time between tests (Schilt et al., 2007).
debate.neither_can_show: The reviews, letters and commentaries describe individual studies in ways that differ from one another and, at points, from the studies' own tables. Only the Dutch cohort tested people before they started, after very little use, and its brain-imaging results are known here only second-hand; no other design read here can separate a difference that follows use from one that preceded it. Binding signals and test scores are surrogates: both can change without any loss of nerve cells, and neither side reports post-mortem or structural evidence in people. Group averages are reported without saying how many individuals fall outside the normal range, and the reviews report no formal assessment of publication bias. The two sides also select differently: the review omits the published critiques, and the commentary omits the transporter imaging studies.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). From the sources read so far (five primary studies and reviews read in full, and the narrative reviews and letters), two things are well attested: a measurable difference in serotonin transporter binding between people who use ecstasy and people who do not, found by several groups, and a modest average difference in memory and executive test scores. Neither establishes lasting damage to nerve cells, and neither is shown to be caused by ecstasy: the designs cannot do it, the exposure is self-reported, and other drug use and pre-existing differences run in the same direction. The strongest argument on the yes side is the relation of both measures to lifetime use; the strongest on the no side is that the one study designed to remove confounding by other drugs found almost nothing, and that the traits in question predict who starts using. The authors on both sides agree that prospective studies are needed, which is the clearest signal of where this stands.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts that measure serotonin transporter binding and cognition in people before first use and repeatedly afterwards, with use verified biologically, a retested group who do not start, and pre-specified outcomes; repeat scanning of the same people over years of abstinence to see whether binding and scores change together; within-person studies of controlled administration with the same measures; and post-mortem studies of structural markers in people with documented long-term use. None of the sources read here reports any of these.
